Baby & Child

Dextrocardia: understanding a right-sided heart

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Dextrocardia means the heart developed with its tip pointing toward the right side of the chest. It is present from birth. Hearing that a baby’s heart is on a different side can be unsettling, but the position alone does not tell you how well the heart works. Some children have no other problem; others need care for conditions affecting the heart, breathing, spleen or intestines.

What does isolated dextrocardia mean?

A right-sided heart can have healthy chambers, valves and blood flow. When an assessment finds no associated heart defect or organ disorder, the term isolated dextrocardia may be used. In that situation, the unusual position itself may cause no symptoms and need no treatment.

The important point is what the examination and scans show. The word dextrocardia describes orientation; it should not be treated as a complete explanation of a child’s anatomy. Ask the cardiologist whether the heart’s connections and function are normal and whether any other findings need follow-up.

How situs inversus and heterotaxy differ

Sometimes the heart is part of a mirror-image arrangement of organs, called situs inversus. For example, the liver may be toward the left and the spleen toward the right. When the major chest and abdominal organs have this reversed arrangement, the term situs inversus totalis is used. A different position does not automatically mean an organ works poorly.

Heterotaxy describes a more complex disturbance of the usual left–right arrangement. It is not simply another name for a mirror image or for any combination of organ abnormalities. Heart connections, blood vessels and abdominal organs may develop differently, and some organs may be absent or function abnormally. This is why two children described as having a right-sided heart can need very different care.

Why can the heart develop on the right?

The difference arises during early development before birth, when the body establishes its left and right sides and the heart takes shape. In an individual child, a precise explanation may not be found. Some associated conditions have genetic causes, so family history and the other findings may guide a discussion about genetic assessment.

A heart can also be pushed or pulled toward the right by a problem outside it, such as an abnormality involving the lungs, diaphragm or chest. This displacement is called dextroposition and is different from a heart that developed with a rightward orientation. Clinicians distinguish the two because the cause and the investigations may differ.

Symptoms depend on the associated condition

A child with a structurally normal, well-functioning right-sided heart may have no symptoms. The position may be noticed on a scan done for another reason. In other children, an associated heart defect affects circulation and may cause fast or difficult breathing, blue or grey colouring, unusual tiredness, tiring during feeds or difficulty gaining weight.

These effects are not explained simply by “too little oxygen in the heart.” Depending on the defect, blood flow to the lungs or body may be altered and the heart may have to work harder. Feeding and growth can suffer. New symptoms need assessment even if an earlier visit was reassuring.

Yellow skin or eyes can indicate jaundice and should also be assessed. In a child with a complex organ arrangement, liver or bile-duct problems may be relevant, but jaundice is not an inevitable effect of dextrocardia. A jaundiced baby who is very sleepy, feeding poorly or passing pale stools or dark urine needs prompt medical attention.

Why some children have repeated respiratory infections

Some people with reversed organ positions also have primary ciliary dyskinesia, or PCD. Cilia are tiny moving structures that help clear mucus and trapped material from the airways. When they do not work properly, ongoing cough and repeated ear, sinus or lung infections can occur. PCD with situs inversus is often described as Kartagener syndrome.

This association does not mean that every child with dextrocardia has faulty cilia, a weak immune system or a tendency to pneumonia. Persistent wet cough, troublesome congestion or repeated infections are reasons to ask whether a respiratory assessment is needed. The position of the heart cannot diagnose PCD by itself.

Heart-wall defects and problems involving the spleen

Associated heart differences can include openings in the walls between chambers. An atrial septal defect involves the upper chambers; a ventricular septal defect involves the lower chambers. Other children have valve or major blood-vessel abnormalities. These can alter blood flow, and a clinician may hear a murmur. The precise defect and its effect on function determine what happens next.

In some forms of heterotaxy, the spleen is absent, small or not working properly. The spleen helps defend against certain infections, so impaired function can increase the risk of serious bacterial illness. A child can also have several small spleens whose function still needs assessment. Neither a right-sided heart nor an unusual spleen position alone establishes how well the immune system is working.

What an assessment may involve

The care team reviews symptoms, feeding, growth and family history and examines the child. Imaging helps distinguish the heart’s location from its internal structure. An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to examine chambers, valves, connections and blood flow; an ECG records the heart’s electrical activity. Chest X-ray, MRI or other imaging may be selected when needed.

If there are signs of a wider organ-arrangement condition, the team may also investigate the abdomen, spleen function or breathing problems. Not every child needs every test. Keep a copy of the diagnosis and relevant scan reports, and tell new healthcare professionals about the heart’s position before tests or procedures.

Treatment is directed at the problem found

There is usually no need to move a healthy heart to the other side. If a structural defect is present, treatment may involve monitoring, medicines, a catheter procedure or surgery, depending on that defect. A repair to a heart-wall opening addresses abnormal blood flow; it is not a standard operation for everyone with dextrocardia.

A pacemaker is relevant to particular electrical or rhythm problems, not simply to a heart being on the right. Ask the cardiologist what each proposed treatment is intended to improve, how urgent it is and what follow-up will be needed. Children with more complex disease may need several specialists working from a shared plan.

Preventing infections when there is a specific risk

If the spleen is absent or works poorly, the team may prescribe regular preventive antibiotics and recommend a vaccination schedule suited to that risk. Families also need clear instructions about fever and other signs of serious infection. Preventive treatment reduces risk but does not make a new fever safe to ignore; follow the child’s urgent-care plan promptly.

For PCD, care focuses on clearing airway mucus and preventing or treating respiratory infections. A respiratory specialist may recommend airway-clearance techniques and antibiotics for selected circumstances. These treatments should not be prescribed automatically to every child with dextrocardia. The reason for infection risk, and the length of any treatment, must be established individually.

When intestinal problems need urgent care

An associated condition can involve intestinal malrotation: the bowel did not rotate and settle in the usual arrangement during development. Malrotation can allow the bowel to twist, called volvulus, or contribute to obstruction. A heart on the right does not mechanically cause the bowel to twist; these findings can occur together as part of a wider developmental condition.

Obstruction stops intestinal contents moving normally. A volvulus can also interrupt the bowel’s blood supply and become life-threatening. Green vomit, severe abdominal pain, a swollen abdomen or a rapidly worsening child needs urgent emergency assessment. Do not wait for constipation to appear or for a routine appointment. Suspected volvulus may require urgent surgery; other findings are managed according to specialist assessment.

What can life be like as a child grows?

Children whose dextrocardia is uncomplicated can grow up with normal heart function and a normal life expectancy. In a more complex case, the outlook depends on the specific heart, respiratory, immune or intestinal problems and the care available for them. The diagnosis alone cannot predict a child’s future health.

Ask which activities are suitable, which appointments matter, and which changes should trigger a call or emergency visit. Keep feeding and growth concerns on the agenda, along with infection prevention when relevant. A short written care summary can help caregivers and new clinicians understand the child’s anatomy without assuming that every symptom comes from the right-sided heart.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pediatric cardiac resources distinguish heart position from the defects or syndromes that may accompany it. Assessment should explain the child’s actual anatomy and function before decisions about monitoring, medicines or surgery are made.

Specialist guidance for PCD and spleen dysfunction supports targeted infection care. A child who has one of these conditions needs an individual plan; dextrocardia alone does not establish the need for long-term antibiotics.

How BeMama can help

Use a care record to keep the exact diagnosis, specialist contact details, appointment questions and the child’s agreed warning signs together. Bring that information to the care team rather than relying on a general description of a right-sided heart.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for blue or grey lips or tongue, severe breathing difficulty, collapse, green vomit or severe abdominal pain. For a child with absent or poorly functioning spleen, follow the fever emergency plan immediately. Contact the care team about poor feeding, faltering growth, repeated infections or jaundice, and seek urgent help if the child is unwell.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A right-sided heart may work normally; associated defects or syndromes determine the care needed.
  • Situs inversus, heterotaxy and displacement of the heart are different findings.
  • Ciliary dysfunction, spleen problems and intestinal malrotation affect some children, not everyone with dextrocardia.
  • Treatment targets a specific problem, and families need an individual follow-up and emergency plan.

Frequently asked questions

Is a heart on the right always dangerous?

No. When its structure and function are normal and there are no associated problems, the position may not affect health. An assessment is needed to establish that this is the situation for a particular child.

What causes dextrocardia?

It begins during early development before birth. Some associated disorders have genetic explanations, but the reason is not always identified in an individual child. A family history or additional findings may make genetic advice useful.

Is dextrocardia the same as situs inversus?

No. Dextrocardia describes the heart’s rightward orientation. Situs inversus describes a reversed arrangement of organs. They can occur together, but knowing the heart’s position does not tell you where every other organ is.

Does every child need heart surgery?

No. Surgery is considered for particular associated defects, not for the right-sided position alone. Some children need no treatment for the position, while others require monitoring, medicines, procedures or surgery for additional problems.

Will my child get more chest infections?

Not necessarily. Repeated infections can occur with associated PCD or certain immune problems, but they are not an automatic consequence of dextrocardia. Persistent wet cough or repeated infections should be discussed with the care team.

Why might a doctor check the spleen?

Some organ-arrangement conditions can involve an absent or poorly functioning spleen. That changes infection risk and may require preventive antibiotics, additional vaccination planning and urgent assessment of fever.

Why is green vomiting an emergency?

Green vomit can indicate a blockage beyond the stomach. A twisted bowel can lose its blood supply quickly. Seek emergency assessment rather than assuming it is a usual stomach upset.

Can a child with dextrocardia live a normal life?

Children with uncomplicated dextrocardia can have normal life expectancy. With associated disorders, the outlook and any activity limits depend on the specific findings. Ask the child’s specialists for advice based on their assessment.

Should we tell new clinicians even if our child feels well?

Yes. The heart’s position and any other organ differences can matter when interpreting tests or planning procedures. Keep the diagnosis and relevant reports available for new healthcare professionals.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
